props.title: P.S. I Love You

sections.content: P.S. I Love You stands at the intersection of grief and romantic comedy, following Holly (Hilary Swank) as she processes her husband's death through posthumous letters he arranged before dying. The film sparked a wave of similar "love beyond death" narratives, including The Lake House (2006) and Charlie St. Cloud (2010). While critics initially dismissed it as melodramatic, it's gained a devoted following for its raw portrayal of loss and healing.

sections.content: The film's Irish setting and soundtrack, featuring The Pogues and Lisa Hannigan, creates a bittersweet atmosphere that elevates it beyond standard romantic fare. Director Richard LaGravenese pulls from the tradition of Irish storytelling seen in Once (2007) and Leap Year (2010), where music and location become characters themselves. Gerard Butler's Gerry crafts an emotional treasure hunt that serves as both torture and therapy for Holly, echoing similar themes in Dear John (2010).

What sets P.S. I Love You apart is its unflinching look at the messiness of grief. Unlike sanitized romantic dramas like Sweet November (2001), the film shows Holly's ugly crying, drunk dialing, and inappropriate laughter. This authenticity influenced later grief-centered romances like Safe Haven (2013) and The Best of Me (2014). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Modern Grief Romance

movies.title: Me Before You
movies.slug: A caregiver falls for her quadriplegic patient, exploring love in the face of impossible circumstances

sections.content: The film helped establish a template for how romance movies handle death, influencing works like The Fault in Our Stars (2014) and All My Life (2020). Rather than treating death as just a plot device, these films explore how love persists and transforms after loss. The success of P.S. I Love You demonstrated audiences' appetite for romance that doesn't shy away from difficult emotions.
